TREATIES ON THE GOSPEL OF SAINT JOHN I

Saint Augustine's commentary on the Gospel of Saint John is a classic exegetical work, despite being all sermons preached to the Hippo people. It is a classic work of exegesis in the sense that the rapport between the evangelist and his interpreter is such that it is very difficult for the evangelist to interpret himself differently than Augustine does. Therein lies the classic or imperishable value of the commentary. The substance of the treatises is theological and moral, as is the substance of the Gospel. The Trinity, the Incarnation, the Church or mystical Body, the sacraments (baptism and Eucharist) and morality, the essence of which is charity, constitute the core of the Johannine Treatises, because they also constitute the core of the Gospel. That is why Bossuet said very accurately "that these precious principles of theology, by which Augustine reconciles his eternal divinity with the origin and mission of the Son of God, are the basic part of the literal meaning of the Gospel and as the purest of its spirit 1. The Treatises, however, are not a classic work of exegesis in a rigorously scientific sense, because they are not a cabinet work, so to speak; they are not the work of Augustine as an exegete, since he does not use the resources of the exegesis and his genius with the sole purpose of unraveling the fullness of the meaning of the evangelical text. The Treatises are sermons preached to the people of Hippo, they are the work of Augustine as a pastor or bishop, whose purpose is the edification of his flock in faith and good morals; that is why he uses in them profusely the appropriate means for that purpose, such as example, allegory, metaphor, etc., etc. Landais says, speaking of this work of Augustine, that it is, without a doubt, his work of exegesis, the closest to us and the most consulted. The liturgy in his breviaries, theology in his arguments and spirituality and preaching in his books and sermons exploit this rich and inexhaustible mine of purest gold.

Chronology is the first thing that must be specified to assess the value of the Treatises and determine the degree of perfection in the evolutionary movement of Augustine's thought. In this I do nothing other than obey the wish of the Saint himself, expressed in the last lines of the prologue to his immortal Retractions: "Therefore, whoever reads these works of mine should not follow me on the path of error, but on the path of perfection; for he will see how writing I have progressed in perfection whoever reads my tracts in the order in which they were written. And in order that this can be done, I will try to do so in this work, to the extent that I am able, so that it becomes known. that same order" 1. This problem of chronology has been faced many times, but it has not yet been solved satisfactorily 2. Let's look at the proposed solutions. Augustine reminds his audience of a promise that he will fulfill, God willing, the next day; It is the explanation of the gospel of the dove 17. Does the promise and explanation of the gospel of the dove appear in some of the immediate Ennarrations, either earlier or later? Nothing is said in the seven preceding narrations, and in narration 127 he does mention the dove, but it is to refer to a previous sermon: "I have already explained to your charity why the dove carried a branch with fruit in its beak" 1S. Could these mysterious sermons be identified with some treatises on the Gospel of Saint John? Let us examine treatises 4, 5 and 6. In treatise 4 he presents to Augustine verse 33, chapter 1 of the Gospel of Saint John, a very difficult problem, which he proposes with heavy insistence to his audience, encouraging them to penetrate more and more of its meaning and difficulty; and he also promises to solve it, with the help of God, within a few days 19. This solution, says Agustín, will forever clog the mouths of Donato and all his henchmen. Treatises 5 and 6 are entirely devoted to the complete elucidation of verse 33. Augustine uses, on the other hand, a text that differs from the Vulgate and repeats two words taken from verse 32: like a dove, sicut columba. Ennarration 126 announces that the next day the speaker will fulfill the promise of explaining the gospel of the dove 20. Treatises 5 and 6 develop the entire Augustinian theology of baptism, exposing what the dove made known to John the Baptist. What sermons, in all of Augustine's literary work, can more clearly claim the title of being sermons on the gospel of the dove than these Treatises of St. John? Tractate 4 of Saint John was preached a few days before the narration on Psalm 126, which was explained on the eve of Treatise 5 21. The narration on Psalm 127 follows treatise 6 on Saint John. From these analyzes and from others that could be made, it can be deduced that, indeed, the gaps in the Enarrations about the gradual Psalms are filled with the insertion of the first twelve treatises about Saint John. Do not believe, says Le Lahdais, that the unity is broken: the comments are not diminished in any way. What is done is discover new depths. As a jeweler arranges two handfuls of dazzling precious stones along a necklace and enriches them with new brilliance due to calculated contrasts, so Augustine alternates the Psalms with Saint John and sets the most beautiful texts of Holy Scripture in the commentaries that have flowed from the fullness of his genius. The result of the previous study leads us to other conclusions, namely: 1.*, that the Enarrations on the Gradual Psalms were preached in Hippo, the same as the Treatises on Saint John. Zarb believes that these Enarrations were preached in Carthage. 2. a, that the date of the sermons on the gradual psalms is the same as that of the first twelve treatises on Saint John. The preaching of the Treatises (1-12) lasted more than fifteen days, against Zarb's opinion, taking into account the chronology of the Enarrations and their insertion in the Treaties. According to this chronology, it seems impossible to put the date of treaties 7 and 8 on March 23, 24 or 25. Psalm 120 was commented on on the feast of Saint Crispina, December 5, and it also seems true that the Felix mentioned in narration 127 is identified with Felix of Ñola, whose feast is on January 14, not with Felix of Zarb, whose feast is on December 17. Tract 12 has been preached very close to Easter and, consequently, before April 22, since from 410 to 420 Easter does not fall later. So the Enarrations and the first twelve Treatises of Saint John (27 sermons in total) are preached during four months, December-March. In treatises 5 and 6, as we already said in Marie Comeau's chronology, there are data that confirm his preaching date in January. Treaty 7 and paragraph 127 cannot be very far from them. In fact, this treaty speaks of the themes of treaties 5 and 6, recently developed 23. It is difficult, therefore, for treaty 7 to be two months apart from treaties 5 and 6.

Now, these fifteen sermons cannot be placed either from Tuesday (March 25) to Holy Wednesday (April 2, 413), nor from Sunday (March 20) to Holy Wednesday (April 3, 418); The first, however, is Zarb's hypothesis, and the second, Huyben's hypothesis. Upon arriving here these questions spontaneously arise in the reader's thoughts: In what year? What time was dedicated to its complement? At what pace did the sermons happen? The answer to the first and second questions is deferred for later. Now only the third will be answered. Since treatise 55, a new rhythm appears and successively and unfailingly dominates the explanation of the fourth Gospel until the end. This difference in rhythm between treatises 1-54 and treatises 55-124 is the reason why some go so far as to say that this second part is dictated, not preached. But, despite the undeniable difference between the treaties, there is no shortage of reasons to continue believing that they are true sermons. Le Landais adduces some reasons, namely: that the terms used insistently in these Treatises are characteristic of true sermons and that the term treatise (tractatus), used with preference in these comments on the Fourth Gospel, is, according to the precise technical sense established by Bardy, an oral explanation of the Holy Scripture 2 *. The strongest argument and the one that Le Landais places the most emphasis on is Augustine's testimony at the end of his great work on the Trinity. We must not lose sight of the fact that the rhythm, structure and brevity of this treatise 99 are identical to those of the treatises in this series. Therefore, if this is a true sermon, why should it be said that the others are not? In the first lines of chapter 48 of book 15 of the De Trinitate, Augustine expresses himself thus: "For it is true that in that coeternal, and identical, and incorporeal, and ineffably immutable, and indivisible Trinity, it is extremely difficult to distinguish the generation from the procession, it is enough for those who cannot rise higher to know for the moment what we said about this matter in a sermon that we preached to the Christian people and that we achieved BARDY, O. At that time Augustine came to hear of the discovery (December 26, 415) of the mortal remains of Saint Stephen, of Gamalie] and his son, and of Nicodemus, whose invention casts a splendid light on the person of Nicodemus and brings to light what was hidden or in darkness, namely: the holiness and martyrdom of Nicodemus. Nicodemus became a Christian and died a martyr for Christ. Augustine comments on Jesus' nocturnal interview with Nicodemus in two treatises preached at a time close to Easter. The portrait he paints of Nicodemus in them is summarized in these features: Nicodemus is a man still closed to the light, and who has not yet passed, by virtue of the new birth, from the darkness of night to the light of day, and who does not understand the language of the spirit nor knows how to decipher the words that are spirit and life, and who is ignorant because he is arrogant 28. Augustine at this date was not yet aware of the miraculous discovery of the mortal remains of Saint Stephen, Nicodemus, etc. These treatises 11 and 12 are, without a doubt, before the summer of 416. In treatise 33 Nicodemus appears again on the scene, and Augustine says that Nicodemus, rather than incredulous, was timid: "He came at night to the light, because he wanted to be enlightened, but he feared to be known" 29. Augustine was still unaware of the Palestinian event. It is known, on the other hand, that treatise 27 was preached on August 10. It is likely that the treaty is also from the same month. In treatise 120, regarding the action of shrouding the body of Jesus, Augustine explains the case of Nicodemus. Augustine indicates that in the evangelical text the punctuation separates the words "the first time" (primum) from these others: "carrying about a hundred pounds of a composition of myrrh." Because it is true that Nicodemus came the first time at night to meet with Jesus, as Saint John says in the first chapters of his Gospel. This means that Nicodemus did not come to Jesus only then, but that it was the first time. But later he returned to listen to him repeatedly and ended up becoming his disciple. This is already clear, says Augustine, as has just been demonstrated by the wonderful discovery of the body of Saint Stephen, which almost everyone already knows about. Augustine, then, learned of the good news that Paulo Orosius brought him from Palestine between the preaching of treatises 109 or 111 and 120. Donatism, it is true, was never condemned by the Church as a heresy. Saint Augustine, however, calls this schism a heresy and a sacrilegious error, since, indeed, the schism involved doctrinal errors about the value of the sacraments and later led to a false conception of the nature of the Church. The error of the rebaptizers and the Novatian error were precursors of Donatism. The Donatists, on the one hand, further extremed the error of the rebaptizers, conditioning the validity of baptism to the orthodoxy and morality of the minister. Establishing the principle that a sinner could not validly baptize or ordain, they concluded that the sacraments of baptism and ordination conferred by apostates and traitors were null. Now, since, in their concept, Catholics were nothing more than traitors or children of traitors, they began to practice baptization and ordination with those who had fled from Catholicism to their party. The Donatists were actually called, as can be seen from a long series of passages from Saint Optatus and Saint Augustine, and a multitude of inscriptions that deserve faith, the pure and the saints and the children of martyrs, in opposition to the Catholics, stained, they said, by their communion with the Christians, who bore the stigma of traitors, who, during the last persecution, had handed over to the pagan magistrates, for fear of imprisonment, the Scriptures. Saints entrusted to their custody 53. The Donatists, furthermore, partly renewed the Novatian schism, especially in their puritanical and rigorous conception of the nature of the Church. They said that the true Church, the Church of Christ, is one, holy, catholic, and apostolic, and that Church is ours, not that of the traitors. Regarding the sacraments, it can be said in a general way that the Donatists disapproved of everything that came from the Catholics. Saint Optatus relates that they trampled on the Holy Eucharist, and threw the holy Chrism to the dogs, and destroyed the chalices and altars, and purified the places consecrated to worship. From which it is evident that they did not admit any sacrament of the Catholics. In particular they rejected baptism and orders. The fundamental circumstance that circumscribes Augustine's entire life from the autumn of 388 until his death, 430, is Roman Africa. Augustine, once he returned to Tagaste the year after his baptism, was never absent from his homeland. The Africans imprison him with the chains of love, to the point of not leaving him free to go to Rome even once, despite the ease with which he could do so. He never gave in to the temptation (if he ever had it) to appear at the famous imperial court of Ravenna, where he would have found such easy access, since his religious brothers and even humble ecclesiastics were received there. It is also known that the emperor Honorius convened a council in the year 419 in order to end the Donatist schism and that the emperor himself was careful to address Augustine, as head of the African legation, a personal summons. The Saint, despite that, does not attend. Within Roman or Christian Africa there was a circumstance that required Augustine's care more than any other and that he had more deeply attached to himself: it was his town of Hippo. Ordained priest (391) and consecrated bishop (395), he established his permanent residence in Hippo, his episcopal city, which was among the first-class ports of Roman Africa and whose population at that time was 40,000 inhabitants 62. Augustine did not limit his activity as a preacher to his episcopal city: he frequently went to preach to the African metropolis, Carthage; and in Bulla-Regia, Chemtou, Bizerte, Constantina, Utica, Tagaste, Argentarlo, Vallis, Beseth and Ain Tunga, etc., he also preached 63. The circumstance of being a priest and bishop of Hippo in those crucial moments of Christianity in Hippo and throughout Africa explains Augustine's literary and apostolic work. Saint Augustine, like Saint Justin, has accepted the diabolical origin of pagan cults as an antecedent parody of Christianity designed to prevent souls from going to the new religion. Along with the hypothesis of the demonic origin of pagan cults, Augustine states a fact that was publicly known, and that is that pagan cults make attempts to attract them due to the similarities taken with Christianity. In this sense he refers to the word of a priest of Pollux who gave his god a false air of Christianity, saying: "Polux himself is a Christian. (Tr. 7, n. 6: "Usque adeo ut ego noverim aliquo tempore illius Pileati Priester soleré dicere: et ipse Pileatus christianus est.") 78 The pagans go so far as to want to make Jesus like one of their own, like a sorcerer, like another soothsayer. From these words of Jesus: My hour has not yet come, they deduce that Jesus was subject to the law of Fatality, to the law of Destiny; but he, as he was in the habit of magical practices, knew the means of averting them*. The Christian people of Hippo, as can be seen from the above, still carried in their spirit terrible traces of paganism. pileatus meant the holy Doctor the brothers Castor and Pollux, whom the Greeks called Dioscuri (= sons of Zeus), as the Romans also called them with the nickname Fratres püeatioc, because it was customary to depict them with their heads covered with the pileus, or Phrygian bonnet in the shape of half an egg, whose origin is due, according to mythology, to the fact that their mother, Leda, wife of the king of Laconia, Tyndareus, conceived them Zeus, the two twins being born in a single egg, so they adopted the cap that covers them in the shape of a half egg. Not everyone agrees with this origin of the pileus, as Festus claims it is due to being natives of Laconia, whose inhabitants have the custom of fighting hooded with this cap. The type of the Dioscuri with the attributes of the horse and the pileus survived until the Christian era. Some worshipers of false beliefs persisted in vulgarizing the pagan symbols with. the illusion of reacting against the Christian religion. Thus, the magicians and charlatans mixed pagan images with Christian distinctives to attract the simple and ignorant faithful.

The structure of this commentary, as already said, depends on the nature of each treatise, the audience, its unfavorable circumstances and the exceptional qualities of the commentator. Second consequence: that the commentary is not a rigorously scientific exegetical work, it is not a cabinet work nor can it be, because it is something very different, as it has to be. The audience, on the other hand, was not highly cultured, but rather coarse and ignorant. What great orator is not cut short by such undistinguished attendance? Is it not true that the audience defines the structure of the homily or sermon? Is it the audience for the sermon and not just the sermon for the audience? Augustine's analysis of what Christ says refers to divine and human nature is more explicit than that of John and his early commentators. The Christ of Saint Augustine, like the Christ of John, is Man-God; but what John says of him corresponds as a whole to his total person, while Augustine indicates more clearly and distinctly under what divine or human aspect the different predicates are attributed to him. Augustine carefully analyzes each of the Trinitarian passages in order to refer some to the Word as man and others to the Word as God; and thus in the Gospel there are two groups of texts: those that teach the divinity of Christ and those that look only at his humanity 102.

Augustine is obsessed with fighting tirelessly to defend the mystery of the Trinity in all its dimensions. In addition to the samples presented that indicate this (adoptionism, Sabellianism, Arianism), others can be presented. For now it is enough to indicate one of them. "It is such," says Marie Comeau, "his tenacity in insisting on the unity and simplicity of the divine essence, that some historians, Harnack, for example, have been able to say that Augustine slipped, unknowingly, towards modalism." There is in him, says another historian, a more or less Sabellian modalism, which Augustine himself probably did not realize. But that does not mean that it ceases to exist in the depths of his doctrine. It is true that he defends himself and rejects the heresy of Sabellius and that he does not want to admit, at the same time as the unity of essence, the unity of the divine person'; but the analogies he uses show us that he was not hostile to the doctrines that replaced persons with modes of being and action 103. The first observation that, in my opinion, should be made to Marie Comeau is that she does not specify what divine essence she is dealing with; which gives rise to ambiguities. It is the numerical unity or identity (non-specific) of the divine essence of the three persons. It is true that Augustine insists on this dimension of the Trinitarian dogma, but his insistence on the refutation of the error of those who insist on destroying the Trinity, understanding the divine essence of the three persons in the sense of specific essence, is no less important. Second observation: The second observation is that I do not know why this way of insisting is called exaggerated, when any insistence on coming to conceive better and taste and savor more of the divine what is all our good is always little. Third observation: I am surprised that Marie Comeau affirms that because of this insistence there have been historians who have been able to say that Augustine slipped towards modalism without knowing it. It is clear that they have been able to say it, because the fact is the best proof of its possibility; but, since there is no foundation for that in Augustine (read, for example, among countless others that I omit, book 7 of the De Trinitate and tr. 36, n. 8 and 9, as proof of the assertion), I say that, since there is no foundation, it should not have been said nor is there any rational justification for attributing to Augustine's unconsciousness the making of the errors that he tirelessly and with such irrefutable effectiveness reduces to dust. l0

The bodily fatigue that Christ has deigned to experience at times is considered, above all, as a symbol of this inconceivable humiliation, revealing an even greater humility. The humility of Christ produces in Augustine's spirit a kind of bewilderment of madness. His brilliant intuitions of the spirit and heart surprise in Christ, due to his humility, attractions of such high carats, which lead him to the embrace of Christ, in which the surrender of his entire being goes, and the fusion of his heart with that of Christ. All his work and his life, from his conversion to his death, are as if anointed with the humility of Christ. In the treatises there are many examples of Augustine's madness of love for the humility of Christ and for humility in general. All of his work and life is a continuous example of that madness. The comment he makes on verses 37 and 38 of chapter 6 of the Gospel of Saint John is an example of that madness of love for humility, and it is not just any example, but one of the greatest 118. I do not believe there are many pages of greater height about humility in religious literature than these by the immortal Doctor of Humility. What conclusion follows from all this? The conclusion is that, for Augustine, Christ-Man, Master and Doctor of humility, as he calls it, is the only way to go to Christ-God, to go to the Father. I am the Way, the Truth and the Life. Humble Christ is the way, and exalted Christ is the truth and the life; Christ the man is the way, and Christ God is the Truth and the Life. If, then, Augustine is enamored of the sacred humanity of Christ, how could he not react vigorously against the idea of ​​an annihilation of human nature in Christ, just as he reacted against the idea of ​​the annihilation of his divinity? Christ is God and man. If you confess God and deny humanity, you deny Christ. As, in turn, if one confesses him as a man and denies his divinity, he also denies Christ; That is a denial, both in one case and in another, with consequences that are fearful because they are irremediable 118. If Augustine has insisted so much on proving the divinity of Christ, he has insisted no less on proving his very true and real humanity 119. In the Treatises Augustine speaks of doctrines that deny either the reality of the human nature of Christ or his integrity. Some as well as others are destructive of the mystery of Christ with all its transcendentals. consequences. These doctrines or heresies bear the names of Docetism and Apollinarianism, respectively. Since the end of the 1st century there were heresies that said the earthly human life of the Redeemer, as well as his passion and death, were fiction or appearance. In History these heretics are called Docets. They did not constitute a distinct sect within the many Gnostic sects. Docetism is an idea common to Gnosticism in its Gnostic proliferations. This idea is a consequence of false Gnostic dualism; matter is essential and intrinsically

evil and a principle of filth with which it is impossible for the Deity to establish contact or consortium. Another consequence of this idea is that Christ did not take a true and real body, but rather an apparent and fictitious one; Christ is not a real and true man, but only appearance and fiction. Heretics of this very bad character were, among others, Marcion, Basilides, Apelles, Valentine and the sectarians of Mani, etc. As one modern historian truly says, Docetism was a strangulation of the mystery of Christ and, consequently, of Christianity. In treatise 8, number 5, Augustine confronts, in the presence of his audience, the perfidious Manichean interpretation of the response that Jesus gave to his Mother at the wedding in Cana of Galilee: What is it with you and me, woman? The perfidy of Mani's henchmen wanted to see in that response that Jesus did not have a mother nor could he have one and, therefore, he was not born of the Virgin Mary nor was she his mother. Augustine, a pastor who watches over the purity of the faith of his flock, comes to their defense based on the most truthful and faithful narration of the evangelist. Augustine speaks thus in the presence of his audience: Let no one shake you from faith in what the Gospel says. The Gospel says that the Mother of Jesus was there and also that Jesus gave his Mother this answer. We must defend the truth of these two things, so that the cunning of the devil does not corrupt the virginity of the heart. For these, says Augustine, who pretend to honor Christ in such a way as to deny Him taking on the flesh, do nothing but preach that He is an impostor. They speak this way so that the serpent has possession of man, not Christ. The lie gives possession to the serpent. The truth, however, is given to Christ. Christ is the truth, the serpent did not remain in the truth; but Christ is true in such a way that everything is true in Him: true Word, God equal to the Father; true soul, true flesh, true man, true God, true birth, true passion, true death and true resurrection. Apollinarianism is like the beginning of Christological heresies. These types of heresies, as the word itself indicates, refer to Christ, to the God-Man, and have in common the false explanation of the union between the two natures, divine and human, in Christ. Apollinaris was a staunch adversary of Arius; He defended the divinity of Christ and said that in Him was found the second divine person, the Word, but united to an incomplete human nature. Christ assumed only the body or, at most, the body vivified by the sensitive soul, the human soul, the intellective or rational soul (the human "pneuma"), being eliminated from that body. Christ lacked the intellectual soul. The Word took its place. Two complete natures—here, in this case, the divine and the human—cannot, according to Apollinaris, be united in the person of the Word and constitute a single supposition, Christ. Only my doctrine, he says, safeguards the immutability and impeccability of the Word; impeccability, because, wherever the human "pneuma" is found, the sinful is grafted into it. Immutability, because, if human nature subsists intact in the union, the change has to take place in the divine dimension of Christ; consequences, both inadmissible because they annihilate Christ. This erroneous way of thinking of the heresiarch has as its philosophical foundation the erroneous concepts of nature and person. Augustine does not cease in his battle against these heresies, against these doctrines, already judged as heretical by the Church, and against his sectarians, already eliminated and excluded from its midst as destroyers of the mystery of Christ, that is, of Christianity. Predestination, then, appears as a synthesis or implication of the other mysteries mentioned, because they are subordinate to it and ordered to its temporary realization. The mystery of our incorporation into Christ is the great revelation made by God to Humanity through the ministry of Saint Paul mainly. Augustine, at the historical moment of his preaching on Saint John, had already reached the most perfect assimilation of the Pauline doctrine of the Mystical Body. Augustine fully lived that life of maximum interiority with Christ and in Christ and measured the maximum transcendence of that living unity with the body of Christ, since it is the reason for God's being in us, the reason for our Christianization or divinization, at the same time that its rupture is the denial of the being of God or Christ in. us. "Nothing," says Augustine, "should the Christian fear so much as separating himself from the body of Christ, since, if he separates himself from the body of Christ, he is not a member of it; and if he is not a member of it, he is not quickened by his Spirit; and whoever he is, says the Apostle, let him not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His." 12i. Augustine is the Father of the Church who took the palm from everyone in profound and brilliant mystical intuitions of the mystery of our incorporation into Christ. In the Treatises, as well as in the Ennarrations on the Psalms and Sermons, there is a sowing of Augustinian formulas of Pauline inspiration, which want to be a translation of the highest experiences of mysticism. The union between Christ and the Church, between the Head and its members, between the Husband and the Wife. After Saint Paul, there is no other like Augustine in the creation of formulas that express with such conciseness, strength and fullness of significance Supernatural realities so gifted and of such height. "In the holy and sacred pages," says the Saint, "three nuances or dimensions of Christ are preached: the dimension of Christ as God, as a Deity equal to the Father and coeternal with Him before the incarnation; the dimension of Christ as God-Man and Man-God at the same time, mediator and head of the Church, after the incarnation;

and, finally, the dimension of Christ as whole, complete or total Christ in the fullness of the Church, which is the Head and the Body; and in the fullness of this perfection we are members of this one and perfect man." 125. More Augustine says: "Let us listen now to what the Head asks and to what the Body asks, to what the Husband asks and to what the Bride asks, to what Christ asks and what the Church asks; the two are one. The Word and the flesh are not both one and the same thing; The Father and the Word are both one and identical thing, one and identical reality; "Christ and the Church are both one perfect man, a man in his fullness" 126. With what courage Augustine translates in these expressions the unity or identity between Christ and the Church! He dares to compare it with nothing less than the unity or identity that exists between the divine persons; the perfection of that unity cannot be valued higher. This same truth is repeated by the Saint countless times in his works. His formulas of expression are very strong and of a very daring realism (never as much, of course, as that of the Apostle); but they all seem insufficient to make known how much he knows, through intuitions and mystical experiences, of the incomprehensible mystery of the unity existing between Christ and his Church; a union only inferior to the hypostatic union and to the unity or identity between the three divine persons of the most august mystery. It is beyond all doubt that Augustine, in the fullness of his episcopal life, came to live that loving vitality. eternal mystery of God's love for men, translated in time, in the unity that he wants to exist between Christ and his faithful or the Church. Augustine, in one of those moments of mystical contemplation of the mystery of the unity between Christ and the Church, bursts forth, full of loving thrill and joy.

The conclusions that are deduced from the established premises are those indicated below, namely: 1) that the Church is a divine institution, truly august and sacred; 2) that the Church is also one; There are not two Churches of Christ, but only one; 3) that men have to belong to it as an essential condition to be able to become Christianized or deified and, as a consequence, saved. * * * The discussion that existed between Catholics and Donatists was not about the divinity and unity of the Church of Christ, since both were in agreement on this, but about the criterion that distinguished it. The schismatics saw the discerning criterion in holiness. The bride of Christ—they said—must bear in each member the seal of the purest and perfect holiness. The problem is the following: Is it true that the Baptist did not know Jesus until that moment? If this is so, how do you explain their resistance to baptizing him? Does he not confess: I am he who must be baptized by you? Then he knew who he was. If, then, he knew who he was, how come he says he didn't know? The Eucharist is not only for Augustine the mystery of the real presence of the body and blood of the historical Christ, but it is also the sacrament of his mystical Body. On the altar the immolation of the historical Christ is carried out and his mystical Body or the mystical Christ is immolated together with Him. The Eucharist symbolizes the vital union between Christ and the Church, between the historical Christ and his mystical Body, and is, furthermore, in the current plan of God's supernatural providence, a most effective means for the progressive strengthening of that union until it reaches its perfect consummation, which is the fullness of Christ. The Eucharist, as a symbol of the union of Christians with each other and of Christians with Christ, is one of the dimensions of the Eucharistic mystery that makes the holy Doctor tremble the most with admiration and love. Just as the soul is the life of the body, so also charity, spread in hearts by the Holy Spirit, is the life of the mystical Body of Christ. Two are like the souls or principles of eternal life of that Body: the Spirit of Jesus, or Holy Spirit, and charity. The Spirit of Jesus accomplishes that wonder of wonders which is the identity between Christ and the Church, between the Head and the members, through the inestimable gift of charity, spread in the hearts of men by the same Spirit. Augustine is the Doctor of charity. With the exceptions of John and Paul, there has been no one in the Church who has managed, like Augustine, to reveal with such irresistible attractions the multiple nuances of the inestimable quality of charity. The text of Paul's faith that Augustine quotes most frequently is the following: The charity of God has spread in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Is there a more admirable way to teach the divine origin of love? One of the points on which he has insisted most is the impossibility, for man left to himself, of transcending himself, of leaving himself, to join his brothers. Every man in whom charity dwells is moved by the Holy Spirit, and is so to the extent of his unity with the Body of Christ. Spiritual men are not valued for their extraordinary gifts or charisma, but for their love for the Church, for their love for unity, since to the extent of that love they possess holiness, possess the Holy Spirit and identify with Christ 157. The first Christians were truly one with each other by virtue of unity and charity. The union between the faithful was so intimate and so perfect due to the diffusion of the Holy Spirit in them, that they were not all but one soul and one heart. It is charity that makes so much diversity of desires, tastes and wills disappear into such a wonderful unity that it can serve to understand in some way and by analogy the unity of the persons of the Trinity. Is it a mistake to say that two men have two souls, and three men three souls, and many men many souls? No, because that's the truth. But let them come closer to God and they all have nothing more than a single soul. If, then, many souls, by the fact of being united to God, are nothing more than one

by virtue of charity, and if many hearts through charity are one, what cannot the very source of charity do in the Father" and in the Son? 158 There have been few men who have overflowed so much in love for the Church and have sweated so much in her service as Augustine. The reason is because no one has contemplated with more depth and affection his identification with Christ. To the extent that the Saint delved into the mystical contemplation of this incomprehensible mystery of love, in that same degree was sacrificed for the love of Christ, the man God, and for men, who are Christ himself. The mediator of God and of men, the man Christ Jesus, is head of the Church, and we are its members; and therefore he said next: And for them I sanctify myself (lo. 17,17). Are they myself too? 159 After affirming: And through them I sanctify myself, he added: That they may be sanctified in the Truth, that is, in myself, because the Truth is the Word, which in the beginning was God" 16 °. What mystery of holiness will be, according to this, the Christian grafted into Christ and through Christ himself, being himself Christ? With what extremes of love will he who is one with his only begotten Son be loved by the heavenly Father? Christ himself says that the Father loves them as he loves Him. Augustine comments on these words: He loves them, says Jesus, because he loves me. It is impossible for someone who loves the Son to stop loving the members of the Son, since the only reason for loving the members is love for the Son. The Father loves the Son for his divinity, since he begot him equal to Him. He also loves him for his being a man: The only begotten Word became flesh and through the Lord the flesh of the Word is lovable to the Father. But He loves us because we are members of the Only Begotten...

SUMMARY OF WHAT WAS SAID ABOUT THE MYSTIC BODY The mystery of the incorporation of all humanity into Christ is an incomprehensible and immutable mystery of divine love for men. The perfect accomplishment of this work of supreme transcendence is carried out by the infusion into souls of the charity of Christ. So, when that charity reaches its fullness in souls, they also become the fullness of Christ. All the sacraments cooperate effectively in the realization of this infinite mystery of love, but none cooperates with such effectiveness and strength as the Eucharistic mystery, which by its nature is a mystery of love, unity and perfection. It is not possible to form an idea of ​​its height if you do not know how far it reaches. Do you want to know what heaven and earth are? Creatures. How then, if He did everything for Him and nothing was done without Him? How can the created be governed by Him, if it is nothing more than a passing sound? What is created is life in Him. It can also be read like this: Everything created has life in it. Everything, then, is life, according to this reading. There is nothing that is not your creation. He is the Wisdom of God; and in the psalm it is read: You did everything in Wisdom. If Christ is the Wisdom of God, and the psalm says that you made everything in Wisdom, it follows that everything has been done in Him and through Him. But, dear brothers, if everything is His work and everything is life, then the earth is life, and the sky is life, and the log is life too. We say, it is true, that the log is life, but we think of the log of the cross, which for us is a source of life. Stone is also life. This mode of interpretation is unseemly; The door is opened so that the filthy sect of the Manichaeans can stealthily approach us again and say that the stone has life, and the wall has a soul, and the rope, the wool, and the clothing too. It is his habit to rave like this. And when it is contained and refuted, they show us what they say from the Scriptures, since it is written: Everything made in Him is life. Don't be seduced, read like this: What has been made (put a comma here and continue), in Him is life. What is the meaning of this expression? The earth is his making, but it is not a creature that has life. What is life is the spiritual form, according to which the earth has been made and exists in Wisdom itself. 17. I will explain myself to your charity as best I can. The craftsman builds an ark. The first thing is the conception of the architect, because if not, how can he build it? But the ark as an idea is not the ark that the eye beholds. That one is invisible, this one visible. We already have the ark made; but it does not cease to exist in the artist's mind. The work is the execution of the idea, which remains in the mind of the artist. This artifact can rot, but the original remains in the mind to make a new one. Focus your attention at the same time on the ark as the conception of the craftsman and on the ark as an executed work. As a conception, the ark is life; but it is not as a work already done. And it is because the soul of the craftsman, where these things are before their execution, have life. The same, brothers, can be said of the Wisdom of God. This Wisdom contains within itself the form of everything before it comes out; and therefore, everything produced according to this form has life in the Word, although it does not have it in itself.

The earth and the sky, the moon and the sun, which your sight beholds, exist first in their archetype and in Him they are life, and outside of Him they are soulless bodies. Understand it, if you can somehow; Well, something great has just been said, although not by me or through me, since I am not great, but yes.

8. Therefore he adds: And of his fullness we have all received. And what have you received? And grace for grace. This is how it reads in the text of the Gospels compared to the Greek codices. He does not say: Of his fullness we have all received grace for grace, but he says: Of his fullness we have all received, and, moreover, grace for grace. I do not know what meaning he meant to give to these words: We have received of his fullness, and, furthermore, grace for grace. We have received from his fullness first grace and again grace, grace for grace. What is the grace that we first received? The faith. To walk in the light of faith is to walk in the light of grace. How have we deserved this grace? Why our previous merits? Let no one flatter himself. Let each one enter his consciousness again, scrutinize the most intimate interiorities of his thoughts and review the history of his life. Don't look at what it is now, if it is something anymore. Look rather at what you have been before being that something that you now are. You will see that you have deserved nothing but punishment. If you deserved nothing but punishments, and Christ has come not to punish your sins, but to give you forgiveness of them, it is a grace that He gives you, not a retribution. What is the meaning of the word grace? Free gift. What you have received is not a purchase of your previous merits. The first grace received by the sinner is the remission of his sins. What have you deserved? Ask this question to justice, and it will answer: Punishment. Ask the same question to mercy, and it will answer: Grace. God had already promised this through the prophets. And so, when he came to give what was promised, he gave, along with grace, the truth. How has the truth been shown? For the fulfillment of the promise. 9. What do the words grace for grace mean? By faith we deserve God. We have not deserved the remission of sins. Hence the great gift we have received, despite our unworthiness, is called grace. What is grace? A free gift. What is a free gift? A simple donation, not a reward. If it were due as a reward, it would not be grace. If it was really owed to you, you were good; But the truth is that you were evil, but you believed in Him who justifies the wicked, that is, in Him who makes a godly man out of a wicked man. Think, then, of the punishments that were due to you by law and of what you have achieved by grace.

The first man fell, and all those born inherit from him the lust of the flesh. This is what the Apostle tells us: For one man is death and for another is the resurrection of the dead. By which man death and by which the resurrection of the dead? Don't get ahead of yourself; The Apostle continues and says: As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will revive. Those who are born of him are from Adam and those born by him are from Christ. Why are everyone born in sin? Because there is not one who is not born from Adam. The birth of Adam was a necessary consequence of the condemnation; birth by Christ is an effect of will and grace. Men are not born of Christ against their will, but of Adam they are born independently of his will. Because it is to be feared that the uneducated will judge that there is a contradiction between what was said by Christ and what was said by John. In a place in the Gospel where our Lord Jesus Christ speaks to the disciples about things concerning his person, they propose this question: How is it that the scribes or experts of the law say that Elijah must come first? Our Lord Jesus Christ expressly says that Elijah has already come and that he is John the Baptist himself. John is questioned and declares that he is neither Elijah nor the Christ. And, indeed, as true is the statement that he is not the Christ as that he is not Elijah either. How, then, can we reconcile the statement of the Precursor with the words of the Judge? Is it possible for the Precursor to lie, when what he speaks he has heard from the Judge himself? Why then does the Baptist affirm that he is not Elijah, and the Lord says that yes, that he is Elijah himself? Our Lord Jesus Christ wanted him to be the prefiguration of his second coming, since John had the same spirit as Elijah. What John is in the first coming, Elijah will be in the second. Do you not think that the herald should say: Withdraw, leave the way clear? Although the herald should say: Depart, John says instead: Come. The herald distances the Judge, while John invites them to approach Him. John invites them to approach the humble person so as not to experience him as an exalted judge. I am the voice of him who cries in the wilderness: Make straight the ways of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God. He does not say: I am John, I am Elijah, I am a prophet. What does it say? I am called the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the ways of the Lord. I am this prophecy itself. 8. The messengers were from the party of the Pharisees, that is, from the princes of the Jews, and they asked him again and said to him: Why do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor a prophet? It seemed to them like an act of daring that he baptized, and that is why the question they ask him is equivalent to this: In whose name do you baptize? You are asked if you are the Christ, and the answer is no. You are asked again if you are perhaps his precursor, because it is known that Elijah will precede the coming of Christ, and you also deny this. The question is insisted upon whether by chance you are one of those heralds who precede him long in advance, that is, a prophet, and by virtue of that you have received such power. And you answer that you are not. John was not a prophet. He was more than a prophet. From the Lord is this testimony: What have you gone to the desert to see? A reed that the wind moves? It goes without a doubt that not. Juan is not this. Juan is not one of those that the wind moves. He who is moved by the wind is harassed on all sides by the spirit of seduction. What, then, have you gone to the desert to see? A man who dresses beautifully? John wears a hard habit, that is, a tunic made of camel hair. Those who dress beautifully live in the palaces of kings. You have not, therefore, gone to see a man whom you dress beautifully. What have you gone to see? To a prophet? I truly tell you that yes, this is more than a prophet. The prophets predicted the coming of Christ long in advance. Juan, on the other hand, shows us it already present. 9. Why do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor a prophet? See how someone who could pass for something else gives up his position. He is the one who comes after me, and who has existed before me, and, as I have already said, superior to me and who I am not.

After his baptism, the Lord having already been baptized, there was no reason for anyone else to be baptized with this baptism. But the truth is that many were baptized with this baptism. At the tenth hour he heard: Rabbi (which means Teacher). If the Lord heard Rabbi at ten and the number ten is that of the law, then the teacher of the law is nothing but the giver of the law as well. Let no one say that one gives the law and another1 teaches the law. It is taught by the same person who gives it. He is the teacher of the law and He Himself teaches it. Mercy is on his lips: therefore he teaches the law mercifully; This is what the Scripture says speaking of Wisdom: On his lips the law and mercy. Do not fear that it will be impossible for you to comply with the law. Go to mercy. If it is very difficult for you to comply with the law, use that pact, that writing, those prayers that the heavenly jurist composed for you. 11. Those who have a dispute and want to address a petition to the emperor, look for a skilled jurisconsult to write it for them, lest they formulate the request incorrectly and, instead of getting what they ask for, they are met with punishment. The apostles wanted to make supplications, but they did not know how to present themselves to the God-Emperor, and they said to Christ: Lord, teach us to pray. You, our jurisconsult; You, the advisor, or rather, you who sit with God on his throne, write for us a formula of supplication. And the Lord writes for them a formula of the code of divine law. And in that formula he teaches them how they should pray; but it is a conditional formula. Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors. If you do not ask according to the law, you are guilty. Do you tremble before the Emperor because you are a prisoner? Offer the sacrifice of humility, the sacrifice of mercy, say this supplication: Forgive me, for I too am a nerd. If you say it, do it. What should you do, where should you go if you lie in prayers? You will not have, as they say in courts, neither the benefit of the rescript nor even the rescript itself. It is a rule of judicial law that someone who is fallacious in their demands does not obtain what they request. This norm exists among men, because a man can be deceived, just as the emperor can be deceived in the claims presented to him. You said what you wanted, because the one to whom you explained it does not know if it is true or not: that is why he leaves it to your adversary to show you your guilt. The emperor, since he does not know if you are lying, can only grant you grace; but, if before the judge you are convicted of falsehood, you are immediately deprived of the benefit that you had obtained through the rescript.

But God, who knows the same thing if you lie as if you tell the truth, not only prevents you from deriving any benefit from the judgment, but also does not allow you to supplicate, because you have had the audacity to be false with the truth.

Let us examine it more carefully and it will be seen with the help of the Lord. The Lord says "deceit." Anyone who understands the Latin language knows that there is fraud when one does one thing and pretends to do another. Be attentive to your charity. Dolo is not the same as pain. I make this observation because a large number of our brothers, who know Latin poorly, express themselves in such a way that they go so far as to say: The fraud makes him suffer; instead of saying: The pain. Fraud is fraud, it is simulation. When you have one thing in your heart and say another, then there is fraud. It is like two hearts: one as the breast of the heart, where it sees the truth, and the other as the womb, where it conceives the lie. And, in order that you may see that this is the idol, it is said in the Psalm: Deceitful lips. What are painful lips? The Psalm follows: They speak evil from the heart and from the heart. What are heart and heart, but two hearts? Since there was no fraud in this one, that is why the doctor did not judge him healthy, but he was curable. Because healthy is one thing, curable is another, and incurable is quite another. The sick person, of whom there is hope, is curable; He who is already hopeless is incurable, and he who does not need a doctor is healthy. The doctor, who had come to cure him, saw that he was curable; there was no duplicity in him. Why is there no fold in it? Because, if he is a sinner, he confesses that he is; If, on the other hand, he is a sinner and says he is righteous, is there duplicity in his confession? We have seen a cursed fig tree, because it had leaves, but no fruits. At the origin of the human lineage, when Adam and Eve sinned, they made themselves girdles of fig leaves. These fig leaves are the sins. Nathanael was under the fig tree as in the shadow of death. The Lord saw him, of whom it was said: A light was born to those who sat in the shadows of death. What was said to Nathanael? You, oh Nathanael, ask me: Where do you know me from? You are talking to me now, because Felipe called you. If you are the people of Israel, in whom there is no duplicity, you have already come to know Christ through the apostles, as Nathanael knew Christ through Philip. But His mercy saw you first before you saw Him, when you still lay oppressed by sin. Have we gone first in search of Christ and has it not been He who went first in search of us? Perhaps it was we, the sick, who went to the doctor and not the doctor to the sick? This does not surprise us, because it happens every year and due to its frequency it has ceased to be admirable, and yet it is more worthy of reflection than what was done in the water hydria. Who who thinks carefully about the works of God, by which he rules and governs the entire world, is not stunned with amazement and is as if crushed by the overwhelming weight of so many miracles? The power of any grain of seed is a matter of such greatness that it shudders with fear whoever considers it. But, since men, attentive to other things, do not consider the wonders of God, by which they ceaselessly glorify the Creator, God reserved to perform non-ordinary wonders so that men, who are as if lethargic, awaken with these wonders and worship Him. He resurrects a dead man, and the man marvels. Thousands are born every day, and no one is surprised. However, if carefully examined, it is a greater miracle to begin to be what one was not than to resurrect what one had already been. The same God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ does these wonders through his Word and the same one who performs them governs them. The first miracles are worked by his Word, which is God with Him; and the latter, by his own Word incarnated and made man for us. In the same way that we admire what Jesus the man did, we should admire what Jesus God did. Through Jesus God heaven and earth were made, and all the beauty of the heavens, and all the opulence of the earth, and the fruitfulness of the seas, and everything that is before our sight, all was made through Jesus God. We contemplate these things, and, if we have his Spirit, they please us in such a way that we praise the Artificer. We do not distance ourselves from Him by looking at His works, facing what He did and turning our backs on His Maker. 2. And we see these things and they are within the reach of our senses. Is it not God who by his Word, that is, by his Only Begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, did all these things?

This is so important that there are men against whom the Apostle warns us to be on our guard in the Scripture cited above: I fear that, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so your intelligence will also lose the simplicity and chastity of Christ, who deny the Gospel and proclaim that Jesus is not the son of Mary, and try to justify their error by saying: What is his mother like, to whom these words are addressed: What is it with you and me, woman? They must therefore be answered and it must also be examined why the Lord spoke thus; Do not believe, in your madness, that you have found something that is opposed to the true faith, thereby corrupting the chastity of the Virgin Bride, that is, violating the faith of the Church. In reality, brothers, those who prefer lies to the truth corrupt their faith. Anyone who believes that Christ is honored by denying him real flesh is making him look like an impostor. Those who build lies in men, what do they dislodge from them but the truth? They bring in the devil and cast out Christ; They put the adulterer inside and exclude the Bridegroom from there; They serve as godparents, or better yet, as mediators for the snake. They try with their words to pass the dominion to the serpent and to exclude Christ from it. When does the snake have dominion? When the lie has it. When falsehood is the owner, the snake is. When the truth has dominion, Christ has it. He says it himself: I am the truth; On the other hand, of the devil (the serpent) he says: He did not remain in the truth; there is no truth in it. But Christ is the truth, to the extent that everything in Him is true: His soul is true, and His flesh is true, and He is true man, and true God, and His birth is true, and His passion is true, and His death is true, and His resurrection is true. Just by confessing any of this as false, rot sets in, and the poison of the snake gives rise to the worms of lies and nothing remains uncorrupted. 6. Here is the recommendation that the Apostle makes of it: I am going to show you a more excellent way. Even when I speak the language of angels and men, if I do not have charity, I become like a ringing brass or a clanging cymbal. How is it shown that all nations belong to these two or three metretas? As someone who weighs or values ​​calls two what he previously called three, in order to ponder the mystery. What are these two metretas? Circumcision and the foreskin. The Scripture mentions these two peoples, without omitting any race of men, when it says: circumcision and the foreskin. These two names express all nations; They are two metretas. These two walls come in opposite directions, and the cornerstone, which is Christ, unites them in himself, making peace between God. Let us now show that the three metretas also mean all people. There were three sons of Noah by whom the human race was reproduced. Therefore says the Lord: The kingdom of heaven is like yeast, which a woman takes and mixes with three measures of flour, until the whole dough has fermented. What woman is that but the flesh of the Lord? What leaven is that but the Gospel? What are the three measures but all the nations because of the three sons of Noah? Then the six hydrias, which made two or three metretas, are the six ages of time, which encompasses the prophecy concerning all nations, represented either in two races of men, Jews and Gentiles, according to the distinction frequently made by the Apostle; well in three because of the three sons of Noah. Prophecy, then, is a figure of all people. Because it reaches them, it is called measure in the Apostle's sense: We have received the measure that reaches you. It is expressed like this by evangelizing the people: According to the measure that reaches you.

According to the way Scripture speaks, this is how it must be understood. It has its own language. He who does not know this is overwhelmed and says: How does the Lord have brothers? Did Mary give birth again? No. The dignity of virgins has its root precisely in it. That female could have been a mother; woman, no. This man was given a woman because of her feminine sex, not because of the loss of her integrity. This is seen by the way of speaking of the Scripture itself. As soon as Eve was formed from the rib of man and before he touched her, she was called woman, as you know: God formed her into woman. Who, then, are these brothers of the Lord? Mary's relatives in any degree. How is it tested? By the same Scripture. Abraham's brother is called Lot, who was his brother's son. Read on, and there you will see that Abraham was Lot's paternal uncle, and yet they call each other brothers. Because? Because they were relatives. Jacob had Sir Laban as his paternal uncle, because Laban was the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's mother and Isaac's wife. Continue reading the Scripture and you will also see there that the paternal uncle and his brother's son are called brothers. Knowing this procedure of Scripture, you will see that all of Mary's blood relatives are brothers of Christ. 3. And those disciples were his brothers even more so. Because even those relatives would not be his brothers if they were not his disciples, and without reason they would not be brothers if they did not recognize the Master as their brother. In fact, in a circumstance in which he was informed that his mother and his brothers were away, He, who was speaking with his disciples, said: Who is my mother and who are my brothers? And he stretches out his hands on his disciples, saying: These are my brothers. And whoever does my Father's will, that is my mother, my brother and my sister. Then also Mary, because she did the will of my Father. This is what the Lord exalts in her: that she did the will of her Father, not that her flesh begot the flesh of the Son of God. Take care of your charity. He comes to Jesus at night and says: Rabbi (you already know that Rabbi means Teacher), we know that you are a teacher. You come from God, since no one can do the miracles that you do if God is not with him. Nicodemus was, therefore, one of those who had believed in his name because of the miracles and wonders that they saw him perform. The evangelist had already said before that, when Jesus was in Jerusalem at the Passover festival, many believed in him. Why did they believe? He says it below: Because they saw the miracles he did. What does it say about Nicodemus? That he was a leader among the Jews and that his name was Nicodemus, and that he came to Jesus at night and said to him: We know that you are a teacher come from God. Then he had believed in his name. And for what reason? He says it himself: Because no one can do the wonders that you do if God is not with him. If, then, Nicodemus was among the number of those who had believed in his name, let us see in the person of Nicodemus the reasons why Jesus did not trust himself to them. Jesus speaks to Nicodemus and says: Truly, truly, I say to you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again. Jesus, then, entrusts himself only to the new born. Behold, they9 believed in Him, but Jesus did not trust Himself to them. Catechumens are like that; They already believe in the name of Christ; but Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Let your charity be attentive to the understanding of this truth. It is said to the catechumen: Do you believe in Christ? You already know that the sons of Jacob were twelve, and from them the people of Israel originated. Jacob is Israel. The people of Israel are the twelve tribes, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were three fathers, they were one people. Three fathers who were like the beginning of the people and also a figure of the people that was first and of what is now: The Jewish people were a figure of the people of Christians. There the figure, here the truth; there the shadow, here the reality, according to the words of the Apostle: All this that happened to them was like a figure. These are the words of the Apostle: Everything, he says, was written for us, who find ourselves at the end of the ages. Let your spirit now turn again to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It is seen that in each of them both free and slave women give birth; You see there children of free women and you also see children of slaves. The slave means no good: Cast out, he says, the slave and her son; The son of the slave will never be an heir with the son of the Udder. The Apostle remembers this fact: The two sons of Abraham, says the Apostle, are figures of the two Testaments, the Old and the New. To the Old Testament belong the lovers of temporal things, the lovers of the world; To the New, however, the lovers of eternal life belong. Therefore, that earthly Jerusalem was a shadow of the heavenly Jerusalem, mother of us all and which is in heaven. All this is also from the Apostle. You already know many things about this city of which we are still pilgrims. You have already heard a lot. Something very strange is seen in these births, in these births, in these generations of free women and slaves; four kinds of men are seen in them. Every day's examples prove it. But now turn your consideration to the fathers who have preceded us, and we will see these categories there as well. The good are born from the good; for example, Ananias baptized Paul; And how are bad people born from bad people? The Apostle speaks of preachers who are not in the habit of announcing the Gospel with purity and who, nevertheless, are tolerated in Christian society, and he says: What does it matter? As long as Christ is announced by all means, whether sincerely or not, I rejoice in it. Was the Apostle evil for this reason and did he perhaps enjoy the evil of others? No; The truth was also announced through the evil ones and Christ was announced. If these baptize people similar to themselves, then the evil ones receive baptism from the evil ones. If, on the other hand, those who baptize are like those to whom the Lord gives this warning: Do what they say, but do not do what they do, in that case, the evil ones are those who baptize. The good baptize the bad, like when Simon Magus was baptized by Saint Philip. These four categories of men are, therefore, well known, my brothers. Attention, I want to repeat them again: record them well, count them, warn them and avoid the bad ones and follow the good ones. Those who are good are born from those who are also good when those who administer baptism and those who receive it are good. The wicked are born of the wicked when those who baptize and those who receive baptism live wicked and impious lives. The good are born from the bad when only those who administer baptism are bad. And, finally, the bad are born from the good when only those who baptize are good and those who are baptized are bad. 10. What Nicodemus answers to the Lord is true: an old man cannot return to his mother's womb and be born. He said, it is true, that this could not be, since he was already old, as if it were possible as a child. Look at that snake raised on the tree who suffered the bites of the snakes. That's how it was done. The men were victims of the bites, and they looked and were healthy. What are snakes, do they bite? They are the sins of the mortal flesh. What is the raised serpent? The death of the Lord on the cross. Because death belongs to the serpent, it was symbolized by its effigy. The snake bite is fatal. The death of the Lord is vital. The serpent is looked upon to annihilate the power of the serpent. What is this? Death is looked upon to annihilate the power of death. But what death is that? It is the death of life, if you can say the death of life; ly because it can be said, what is said is admirable. Shouldn't we be able to say what could have been done? Will I hesitate to confess what the Lord was pleased to do for me? Is not Christ the Life? And yet, Christ is on the cross. Is not Christ the life? And yet Christ is dead. But in the death of Christ he found his death. Because dead life killed death; The fullness of life swallowed up death: death was absorbed by the body of Christ. This is what we will say in the resurrection, when in triumph we sing: Where is your power, O death? Where is your sting, O death? Now, in the meantime, brothers, that we may be healed of sins, let us look at Christ crucified; For just as Moses, he says, lifted up the serpent in the desert, so it is fitting that the Son of Man be lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life. Just as those who looked at that serpent did not die from its bites, so those who look with faith at the death of Christ are healed from the bites of sins. But those were freed from death to live temporary life, but here it is said that they live eternal life. This is the difference between the figurative sign and reality itself. The figure gave only temporal life, while the very reality of that figure gives eternal life. 12. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but so that the world might be saved through Him. For the doctor as such comes to cure the sick. He who refuses to observe the doctor's prescriptions puts himself to death. The Savior has come into the world. Why is he called Savior of the world, if not to save it, not to condemn it? Don't you want Him to save you?

By your conduct you will be judged. But what do I say: will you be judged? Look what it says: He who believes in Him is not judged; but he who does not believe... What do you expect to be said except that you will be judged?

In none; in all bad. How is it that some practiced the truth and came to the light? There are many, then, who love their sins and many also who confess them. He who confesses and accuses himself of his sins makes peace with God. God reproves your sins. Always be vigilant, my brothers, for your health; always be awake while time lasts. No one arrives late to the temple of God, nor lags behind in the work of God, nor draws back from continuous prayer, nor allows himself to be robbed of the usual fruit and piety. Stay awake while the day lasts and the day shines. Christ is the day. Christ is willing to forgive, but those who are recognized and punished; but not to those who defend themselves and boast of their justice and believe themselves to be something when they are nothing. He who walks in his love and in his mercy, now free from those mortal and great sins, such as crimes, and homicides, and thefts, and adulteries, does not stop doing the truth and coming to the light with good works, confessing sins that seem small, such as those of the tongue, or of thought, or of the lack of moderation in lawful things, since many small sins, when neglected, kill. Very small are the drops that fill the rivers, and the same can be said of the grains of sand: if the load is great, it oppresses and crushes. The careless bilge produces the same effect as the impetuous waves; The water gradually enters the bilge, but, entering for a long time and not emptying, it eventually sinks the ship. What is emptying the drain but doing good works, such as groaning, and fasting, and helping, and forgiving so as not to be crushed by the weight of sins? How difficult is the path of this century and how full of trials so that man does not become arrogant in prosperity nor dejected in adversity! Whoever grants you the happiness of this century, grants it to you for your consolation, not for your corruption.

Likewise, whoever spanks you in this century does so to correct you, not to lose you. Suffer the father who teaches you, so that you do not experience him as a judge who punishes you. Every day I am telling you this, and it is good that it be repeated many times, because it is a good and healthy thing.

This lesson of the holy Gospel teaches us the excellence of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ and the humility of that man who deserved to be called the friend of the Bridegroom, so that we may know the difference between a man who is only a man and a man who is also God. For the God-man, our Lord Jesus Christ, God before all ages and man in our century, God who is born of the Father and man who is born of the Virgin, is, however, one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, God and man. But John, exceedingly graced, is sent before Him and illuminated by him who is the light itself. Of John it is said: It is not he who is the light, but he who bears witness to the light. It can be called, without a doubt, light and rightly it is called itself. But illuminated light, not illuminating light; because the light that illuminates is one thing, and the light that is illuminated is quite another. Our eyes are called Luceros, and yet they are open in the darkness and see nothing. The light that illuminates is light by itself, and it is light of itself, and it is light that does not need another light to shine, while all the others need it to shine. 2. You have already heard, then, the confession that John made; Because, as Jesus had more disciples every day, they went to John with this news to instigate him, and, as if it were a man who was envious, they said to him: Look, that one has more disciples than you! John confessed what he was, and that is why he deserved to be Christ's, because he did not have the audacity to say that he was the Christ. This, then, was what John said: Man cannot receive anything if it is not given to him from heaven. Therefore Christ gives and man receives. You yourselves are witnesses of what I said: I am not the Christ, but the herald who precedes him. The one who has the wife is the husband; but the friend of the Bridegroom, who stands to hear him, is filled with joy at the voice of the Bridegroom. He did not want to 'rejoice in himself or of himself. Whoever wants to rejoice in himself and himself will always be sad; On the other hand, whoever wants to rejoice in God and of God will be joyful eternally, because God is everlasting. Do you want your joy to be everlasting?

Hear another testimony. You know the great number of those who embraced faith when they placed the price of all their assets at the feet of the apostles so that it could be distributed to each one according to his needs. What does Scripture say about that assembly of saints? They had, he says, one soul and one heart in the Lord. If charity makes so many souls one and so many hearts one heart, then how great will be the charity between the Father and the Son? Without comparison, greater than that which existed among those men who had only one heart. If the heart of many brothers is one through charity and the soul of many brothers is one through charity, will you dare to say that God the Father and God the Son are two? Because, if there are two Gods, charity between them is not sum.

Because, if charity here reaches the point of making your soul and that of your friend a single soul, how is it possible that God the Father and God the Son are not one God there? Unfeigned faith is very far from this thought. In short, to what height this charity rises above the rest, gather from here: The souls of many men are many.

Carnal thought does not understand what I say. Let him leave understanding until later and begin first with faith, and let him hear what follows: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; But he who disbelieves the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God abides in him. He did not say that the wrath of God comes upon him, but that the wrath of God remains in him. All those born into this mortal life carry within themselves the weight of God's wrath. What wrath of God is that? The one that the first Adam suffered. When the first man sinned and heard: You will die without a doubt, he became subject to death and we began to be born mortals: We are born with the wrath of God. From there (from heaven) came the Son, who had no sin, and put on flesh, put on mortality. If He shared with us the wrath of God, will we be lazy in sharing with Him the grace of God? Therefore, whoever does not want to believe in the Son, bears the weight of God's wrath upon himself. What wrath of God? The same one that the Apostle speaks of: We too were by nature children of wrath, like everyone else. We are, therefore, all children of wrath, because we are all born with the curse of death. Believe in Christ made mortal for you, so that you may see him immortal; because, when you see his immortality, you too will cease to be mortal. He was alive and you were dead; He dies so that you may live. He brought us the grace of God and freed us from his wrath. God defeated death so that it would not defeat man.

I will not stop here in long disquisitions on this evangelical text, which is clear and manifest, for fear that I will lack time to delve deeper and explain more obscure things. Certainly, if the Lord saw that the. Pharisees were interested in knowing about the disciples he made and the many he baptized with the intention of following him, for their health, and to become his disciples and to be baptized by him, he would not have left Judea so soon, but would have stayed there for them; But Jesus, at the same time that he realizes what they knew, also realizes their envy: they tried to find out what Jesus was doing, not in order to follow him, but in order to persecute him; That's why he left there. He could, without a doubt, remain there without being arrested by them, if He did not want to, and without being able to kill him, if He did not want to, as he could not have been born if that had not been his will. Perhaps this expression of the evangelist worries you: Jesus baptized more than John* And after having said that he baptized, he added: Although Jesus did not baptize, but his disciples. What then? Is the first statement false and did you have to rectify it by adding this other one: Although Jesus did not baptize, but rather his disciples? Or are both true: that Jesus baptized and that Jesus did not baptize? Jesus baptized, because it was He who purified; and he did not baptize, because it was not He who immersed in the water. The disciples exercised the corporal ministry, and the Master provided the help of his majesty. How could I stop baptizing and never stop purifying? The same evangelist John says of Him through the person of the Baptist: This is the one who baptizes. Then Jesus continues to baptize and will continue to baptize as long as there is someone who needs his baptism. Let the man approach the inferior minister with confidence, because there is a teacher who is much superior to him. 4. But someone may say: Christ baptizes, yes, spiritually, but not bodily. Pay close attention to the Apostle: Like Christ, he says, he loved the Church and gave himself up for her, purifying her with baptism of water and with the word to present her before himself full of glory and without spot or wrinkle or anything similar. He had, therefore, says the Evangelist, to pass through Samaria.
